extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, social science methodology, and scientific inference (e.g., sociologists, political economists, philosophers of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying methods of scientific inference to social/political phenomena, describing limits of inductive and deductive methods and the role of verification. Emphasizes how plurality and intermixture of causes affect causal inference and theory-building in sociology/political science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Method of Difference in social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Difference (eliminating antecedents to find a single cause) is completely out of the question for social phenomena when plurality of causes prevails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an effect admits of several causes, eliminating some antecedents does not prove that an eliminated circumstance was not sometimes instrumental; one can only conclude that the effect is sometimes produced without it. Therefore do not infer single causation from instances where many causes could jointly operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited value of the Method of Agreement under plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding multiple instances that agree only in one antecedent raises only a trifling presumption of causation when many causes can produce the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a set of prosperous nations only share a restrictive policy, that coincidence by itself gives almost no weighty presumption that the restrictive system caused prosperity. Be skeptical of claims of causation based solely on agreement across complex social cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: When many causes jointly influence social attributes, aggregate variations will not bear a uniform proportion to any single component cause, undermining concomitant-variation inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If different agents do not produce qualitatively different effects and quantities are mixed results of many agents, you cannot reliably assign variation in the aggregate to variation in one constituent cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues: useful but presupposes known causes and deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Residues attributes the unexplained remainder of an effect (after accounting for known tendencies) to other known circumstances, but presupposes that some causal tendencies are already known—often by a priori deduction from human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use residues only after allowing for causes whose tendencies are known; recognize it is not pure empirical induction but relies on deduction from general laws of human nature, with experience as a supplementary check. Do not treat it as definitive without theoretical grounding and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simplistic Chemical/Experimental method for complex social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the experimental/chemical method (seeking single causes via controlled elimination akin to chemistry) to political/social phenomena is a gross misconception because social effects are produced by many cooperating causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to treat social phenomena as if a single cause produces a given effect in all instances. Avoid overreliance on simple experimental analogies when investigating complex social sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid geometrical/abstract (monistic) deductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating social science like geometry—deducing consequences from one or a few universal axioms (so that truths are absolute and non-conflicting)—is erroneous because social phenomena result from multiple, potentially conflicting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construct political theories from single abstract maxims (e.g., 'government founded on fear' or 'abstract right') or treat rules of conduct as prior axioms for theory. The deductive basis must account for the plurality and interaction of human motives and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject single-premise political explanations (e.g., pure self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory that explains rulers' or societies' conduct solely by one factor (such as private/selfish interest or responsibility to the governed) is excessively narrow and often false; many other habitual sentiments, traditions, and class characteristics influence conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political theories, include influences such as traditions, maxims of predecessors, communal sentiments, duty, and class habits. Recognize that responsibility may be practically important but is not the only or universal means of aligning rulers' interests with the governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete Deductive Method for sociology (deduction from many premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sociology should be deductive like the complex physical sciences: deduce effects from the laws governing separate elements (laws of human nature), compounding many causal tendencies rather than relying on one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using deduction, consider all relevant causes and compound their tendencies. Accept that, due to complexity, deductions will often yield tendencies rather than precise quantitative predictions. Use the method with adaptations and precautions suited to social complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification is an essential constituent of the deductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive conclusions must be collated with concrete phenomena or empirical laws; the concurrence of a priori deduction and a posteriori observation is the real ground for confidence in sociological conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always verify deductive results against observation. In complex cases the order may invert (derive conjectures from experience, then connect them to human nature by a priori reasoning), but both deduction and verification are required for reliable knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological inference yields tendencies not precise predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct deduction in sociology can establish tendencies—what a cause will tend to produce unless counteracted—but cannot usually determine the exact magnitude or whether it will be counteracted, because of innumerable coexisting agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sociological conclusions as guidance to influence tendencies and to take precautions, not as infallible predictive formulas. Policymaking should aim to surround society with circumstances whose tendencies are beneficial, while acknowledging uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of the inverse method (empirical-first) in complex cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In prodigiously complicated sociological inquiries where direct deduction is inapplicable, begin with empirical generalizations from historical/specific experience and subsequently connect them to principles of human nature by deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When empirical laws can be obtained, employ the inverse method (induction from history then theoretical connection). Reserve direct a priori deduction for cases where empirical laws are unobtainable or where principles are clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of laws: account for pervasive mutual influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every element of the social state more or less influences every other; there is pervasive intermixture of laws, so no social phenomenon can be fully understood in isolation from the rest of the society's condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing any social feature, take into account its relations with other elements of society and all causes influencing those elements. Avoid treating phenomena as isolatable without considering systemic interdependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of breadth in theoretical foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a science from only a few agencies and leaving the rest to practice or conjecture is unphilosophical: you will misestimate omitted causes and give disproportionate attention to those included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to include as many materially determining agencies as practicable in theoretical foundations. If omitted factors are significant, their exclusion will distort deductions and policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of à priori calculation in social theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the complexity and unknown coexisting agencies, à priori calculations cannot compute with precision the mutual action of many social forces; at best they can distinguish tendencies and relative strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect precise numerical or fully determinate outcomes from pure deduction. Use a priori reasoning to identify directions of tendency and relative potency, and rely on verification/empirical rules to refine understanding.
